i assume you mean a speaker using several identical drivers, compared to a speaker with one driver.

Generally, it sounds better. You can achieve same sound pressure level with fewer watts which leads to better linearity (generally speakers have lower distortion with lower output levels: they sound better at low volume). Phase alignment is an issue, though. The other downsides are physical size and cost.

A megaphone has two effects on a human voice.

First, it filters out the low and high frequencies, so that you hear only the middle (harsh) frequencies. Like the sound of an old telephone or a small speaker radio.

Second, and most important for your question, it distorts the audio signal slightly. Simple audio (1 tone) looks like this:

Sine wave

Normal audio (a song, your voice, a sound) is a mix of hundreds of different sine waves, and looks like this:

Audio wave

If you could look closely, and a computer can, you would see sinus waves of various frequencies in the above wave form, all superimposed on one another.

The amplifier in a megaphone does this:

Slightly clipped

You might notice that the wave is amplified so that soft sounds become audible, but to a point where the hardest sounds (the peaks in the wave) are too loud for the speaker system. Those peaks are 'cut off', or 'clipped', which looks like someone hacksawed the top and bottom of your waveform, and which sounds like distortion.

If you would pass a sound through a series of megaphones, the signal would repeatedly be amplified and cut off, which would result in this:

Heavily clipped

where the audio wave form is barely recognizable, as is the sound.

Distortion can be put to good use. Really good tube mics can introduce some distortion in a vocal, which can make it sound sweeter. Every distorted guitar does the above. A Fender Rhodes piano with some distortion sounds really nice. And there would be no grunge, heavy metal, rock, etc, without distortion.

Progressive rock. It still has a huge cult following (I myself am a gigantic fan) and there are still plenty of prog rock bands forming all the time, but after the 70s, when bands like Yes and Genesis changed their style from prog to pop, it lost a lot of mainstream popularity.

Progressive rock definitely received backlash, with punk rock being developed as a minimalist reaction. Prog rock was viewed as too long-winded, synthy and indulgent. Punk icon John Lydon notably wore an "I Hate Pink Floyd" shirt (even though he really liked them).
